questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Going to a destination with a different culture than the Danish, and in an area of Europe, where I didn't have much knowledge.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. I received all the information needed in good time before my arrival. The professor, in charge of the Erasmus-programme at the host-university, reached out to us and gave us a digital guide with a lot of information, which provided all the help I needed.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Besides the information handed to me digitally, we had a meeting at the faculty, where we were introduced to the place. This meant information about studying at the university, living in the city and other useful information. We received contact information for different people, who we could reach out to, if we had questions/needed help regarding studying, social life or other things.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
There are a lot of different websites, where it is possible to find housing. Its not hard to find a good place to live within reasonable pricing, and the city is big with a lot of interesting areas, each with their own pros/cons. 
If you start looking for accommodation 2-3 months before arriving, then you should be able to find a proper place to live for a good price.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is an opportunity to have a bigger influence on your housing situation. You can decide to live with the roommates you want, you can decide to live on your own, you can pick a specific area of the city, and you get the chance to have an impact on the interior design of your home.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The process was divided into two phases. The first phase, where courses were distributed randomly among the students registering for the specific course. In the second phase, we could apply for new courses, if we didn't get the courses we applied for in the first phase. In this phase, the courses were distributed by the principle of first come first served.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: We could always reach out to the university if we had questions about the process, how to manage our time-table, or if we wanted to change courses after already choosing some.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Some courses were cancelled, some were conflicting with each other's timetables, and others had a very limited amount of students able to participate, which meant that I had to reconsider and find courses did I didn't expect to participate in before leaving Denmark.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be open to courses you didn't expect to participate in before leaving Denmark. Write the university if you are really dependent on a specific course or if you made a mistake in the registration process.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Every course is 5 ECTS points, which meant that the courses are quite small compared to the usual size of courses at the university in Copenhagen. The expected preparation time is way below what I have been used to, and the level is, in general, below what I have seen at Copenhagen University.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: At my host university, most of the teaching was like a lecture at UCPH. This means that the style of teaching is less active for the students. Usually, the students at the host university do not have to prepare anything for the classes, which means that the preparation for classes only exists of reading the provided material.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- The Law of the Internal Market 1.
- Civil Liberties in the United States
- Multinational enterprises and private international law
- Current challenges in international, European and Hungarian refugee law
- The law of asset planning and asset management
- Chapters from the History of Constitutional Adjudication

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The law of asset planning and asset management:
- This course gives a comparative look on asset-legislation around the world. The course is a good way of touching upon a new area of law, which does not play the biggest role on the bachelor at UCPH.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not really encounter any unexpected costs

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Groceries are in general not as cheap, compared to the prices seen in Denmark, as they were just 4-5 years ago. 
Public transportation is really cheap as student - both inside and outside of the city.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
A lot of sports clubs organized by the university in many different types of sports. 
The Erasmus organisations makes a lot of social events for Erasmus-students from all over the city. This could be hikes, trips outside of the city, parties, movie-nights, museums days, visiting local restaurants etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Participate in a sports club:
Its a good way to meet people in the beginning of you stay. This makes sure that you meet people in different contexts and it is also a great way of meeting locals.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
There is a lot of good towns within a few hours of Budapest. Many of them are close to interesting nature areas, and visiting the towns are often a better way of getting a broader impression of the Hungarian people than staying inside the capital. 
For instance:
- Eger, and the Bükk national park
- Visegrad
- Esztergom
- The Balaton lake
- The Tokaj region

There is also good access to other central-european countries, such as Austria, Slovakia, Poland, Rumania and Croatia - all of these countries have interesting sights close to the Hungarian border and can often be reached easily by either train or bus.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer:
It is really easy to adjust to the local culture. I didn't really have any practical challenges with settling and a lot of things work in a way that is similar to Denmark. Some things actually work more smoothly compared to Denmark. 
The introduction period was vital in adjusting to a new country, and especially finding people you like to spend time with when not at the university is important. It makes it much easier to explore the culture when you have good people by you side.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Be active in classes and talk to other students before and after class. 
Participate in a sports club or another type of organization where locals participate. 
Go to parties at locations, where locals would go as well.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The Hungarian language is really different from everything else, and the locals(the professors) do often have an accent in English, which can be a bit difficult to understand at times.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Its a culture which bears marks from big historical events, and this can be seen and felt throughout the entire city. There is a lot to learn about and this often has a greater connection to Europe in general. For instance the current situation with Hungary in the EU, the communist rule in Hungary, the two world wars etc.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Participate in as many social events as possible, especially in the beginning of your stay
2. Follow, prepare for and pay attention to the classes during the semester, in order to have a chill exam period and a good ending to your stay
3. It is really easy to settle and manage the practical stuff about moving to Budapest, so don't stress out about this. The university will also give you all the help and information you need.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure to make a plan for every week and make sure that you don't have to study during the weekend. It was important for me to make the most of the weekend, hence why I made sure that I didn't have to study when I was planning to go on trips etc.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting people from different cultures and sharing experiences and knowledge with them. Getting to live in another country, getting to know a new culture and exploring Central Europe.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding time for all of the things I wanted to do and see.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
